Ares Management has delivered a 70.4% share price gain over the past 5 years, yet the recent pullback and fresh deal activity put a sharper spotlight on one question for investors: Is today's valuation still grounded in the returns the asset manager earns on the capital it puts to work across credit, real assets and infrastructure?

The stock's next move may depend on whether the returns Ares Management earns on its capital are strong enough, and durable enough, to support the price investors are paying today.

The Excess Returns model looks at how well Ares Management turns each dollar of equity into profit above its cost of capital. On the inputs here, the firm is assumed to earn average return on equity of 27.23%, with a stable earnings power of $5.93 per share supported by a stable book value estimate of $21.76 per share. Against a book value today of $11.03 per share and a cost of equity of $1.88 per share, the model attributes $4.04 per share to excess return. This is what gives this approach its punch for asset managers like Ares.

Those economics matter because the Excess Returns projections put Ares Management's estimated intrinsic value meaningfully below the current share price of $121.88. The recent bid for Rio Tinto's $7b power infrastructure assets helps explain why investors may still pay up, since it underlines management's willingness to keep deploying capital into fee rich areas even as the model points to a premium.
